If a step depends on overlapping sets, division, or inequality conditions, check that those operations also work in the smallest induction step.
notation: Base case: verify P(n₀).
Induction hypothesis: take arbitrary k≥n₀ and assume P(k).
Induction step: prove P(k+1) under that assumption.
proof_induction.example: For n≥1, prove 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2. It holds at n=1. If the first k terms sum to k(k+1)/2, adding k+1 gives (k+1)(k+2)/2. Therefore the formula holds for all positive integers.
common_mistakes: Omitting the base case or starting at the wrong index.
Merely rewriting P(k+1) without deriving it from P(k).
Overlooking a failure at the smallest k and claiming the step holds for every k.

proof_induction__induction_principle.title: The base case and successor step
proof_induction__induction_principle.summary: Both a starting case and a transition for every successor are required, with a clearly stated index range.
proof_induction__induction_principle.definition: From P(n₀) and P(k)→P(k+1) for every k≥n₀, one may conclude P(n) for all n≥n₀. The induction hypothesis is used temporarily only while proving the successor step; it does not assert all conclusions in advance.
proof_induction__induction_principle.explanation: If the successor argument works only over a certain range, the required earlier base cases must be covered separately. Checking many numerical examples cannot replace an argument for arbitrary k.
notation: Base case: P(n₀).
Successor step: take any k≥n₀, assume P(k), and prove P(k+1).
proof_induction__induction_principle.example: When proving from n=0 that 3^n−1 is even, check that the value 0 at n=0 is even. Induction need not start at 1.
common_mistakes: Omitting the base case.
Writing the induction hypothesis as “assume the claim holds for all n.”

proof_induction__induction_algebra_inequ.title: Algebraic recurrences and inequalities in induction
proof_induction__induction_algebra_inequ.summary: An inductive step must connect the new case to a known earlier case and check the range in which each inequality applies.
proof_induction__induction_algebra_inequ.definition: For sums, divisibility, and inequalities, one often splits the expression for n=k+1 into the n=k part and a new term, then applies the induction hypothesis. Operations such as multiplying an inequality without changing its direction require checks on signs and index conditions.
proof_induction__induction_algebra_inequ.explanation: Writing the new expression is only the beginning: show exactly where the hypothesis is used and why the resulting bound reaches the new target. Too small a starting point may make the inequality itself false.
notation: S(k+1)=S(k)+the new term.
If c≥0 and A≥B, then cA≥cB.
proof_induction__induction_algebra_inequ.example: From 2^k≥k+1, obtain 2^(k+1)≥2k+2; then use k≥0 to obtain 2k+2≥k+2. Only then is the new target proved.
common_mistakes: Using the hypothesis once and skipping the remaining comparison.
Preserving an inequality’s direction without checking whether the multiplier is negative.

proof_induction__induction_failure.title: Induction gaps and the smallest boundary case
proof_induction__induction_failure.summary: False induction arguments often fail at the starting point, first step, coverage of the range, or through circular reasoning.
proof_induction__induction_failure.definition: Valid induction requires a true base case and a valid successor argument for every permitted k. One counterexample disproves a claim, but diagnosing a false proof also requires identifying the condition it uses invalidly.
proof_induction__induction_failure.explanation: Check the smallest k especially carefully: two subsets may not yet overlap, a denominator may be zero, or a recurrence may refer to an index not yet established. Apparently correct algebra for large k does not justify skipping the boundary.
notation: The smallest inductive step is k=n₀.
Circular reasoning: treating P(k+1) as a known premise when deriving P(k+1).
proof_induction__induction_failure.example: In the overlapping-groups false proof that “any n integers are equal,” the two groups at k=1 are disjoint and cannot connect a₁ to a₂.
common_mistakes: Saying only that the conclusion is false without locating the proof error.
Treating a few correct base examples as evidence that every successor step is valid.

proof_strong_induction.title: Strong induction
proof_strong_induction.summary: When proving the next case, strong induction permits using every smaller index in the stated range.
proof_strong_induction.definition: To prove P(n) for all integers n≥n₀, verify the necessary base cases. Then, for arbitrary k, assume P(j) for every n₀≤j≤k and derive P(k+1). If a recurrence uses two earlier indices at once or decreases by a fixed step size, include enough base cases to ensure that each smaller index used has already been covered.
proof_strong_induction.explanation: Strong induction has the same proving power as ordinary mathematical induction, but is especially useful for prime factorizations, recursive objects, and recurrences depending on several earlier terms. Check that each object used in the step is smaller than the current one and still in the claim’s defined range; unproved boundary cases cannot be borrowed.
notation: Strong induction hypothesis: P(j) holds for every j∈{n₀,…,k}.
Goal: derive P(k+1) from all permitted smaller cases.
An argument decreasing by 3 usually requires three consecutive starting indices.
proof_strong_induction.example: To prove every n≥2 is a product of primes: the case n=2 holds; assume the claim holds from 2 through k. If k+1 is prime, it is done. If composite, write k+1=ab with 2≤a,b≤k. By the strong induction hypothesis, a and b are each products of primes; combine their factorizations.
common_mistakes: Mistakenly allowing only P(k) in the strong induction hypothesis.
Using an index below the starting point or providing too few base cases for a fixed-step argument.
Applying the induction hypothesis to factors without proving they are strictly smaller than the current integer.

proof_strong_induction__strong_hypothesi.title: The strong induction hypothesis and ordinary induction
proof_strong_induction__strong_hypothesi.summary: Strong induction can use the whole established initial range and has the same proving power as ordinary induction.
proof_strong_induction__strong_hypothesi.definition: When proving P(k+1), the strong induction hypothesis provides P(j) for every n₀≤j≤k. Defining Q(k) as the conjunction of these P(j) statements turns strong induction into ordinary induction on Q.
proof_strong_induction__strong_hypothesi.explanation: Strong induction does not assume future cases or permit values before the starting point. It places several previously established smaller objects in the hypothesis together, making it suitable for decomposition and recursion.
notation: Strong induction does not allow direct use of P(k+1).
proof_strong_induction__strong_hypothesi.example: For a property stated for n≥2, the proof for k+1 may use P(2), P(3), …, P(k), but may not use P(1) without justification.
common_mistakes: Replacing “all smaller indices” with an unrestricted “all integers.”
Believing strong induction proves a broader class of natural-number statements than ordinary induction.

proof_strong_induction__recursive_decomp.title: Strong induction by decomposition into smaller objects
proof_strong_induction__recursive_decomp.summary: The induction hypothesis can be used only after the current object is decomposed into strictly smaller objects that remain within the stated range.
proof_strong_induction__recursive_decomp.definition: A recursive decomposition proof establishes the smallest objects as base cases, expresses a larger object as a combination of smaller objects, checks the size and definition conditions for each subobject, and combines their conclusions.
proof_strong_induction__recursive_decomp.explanation: Prime factorizations, binary representations, and recursive constructions can use this structure. A subobject equal to the original object or below the starting point cannot support a valid induction call.
notation: For a composite n=ab, one usually needs 2≤a,b<n.
For n≥2, the integer ⌊n/2⌋ satisfies 1≤⌊n/2⌋<n.
proof_strong_induction__recursive_decomp.example: Divide n by 2 to write n=2m+r, with r∈{0,1}. First handle the smaller m, then increase every exponent in its binary power representation by one and append r.
common_mistakes: Failing to prove that each subobject is strictly smaller.
Applying the hypothesis when a subobject is outside the permitted range.

proof_strong_induction__multibase_induct.title: Multiple base cases and fixed-step recurrences
proof_strong_induction__multibase_induct.summary: A recurrence using multiple earlier terms or decreasing by several steps requires enough base cases to cover every chain.
proof_strong_induction__multibase_induct.definition: If a step derives P(n) from P(n−d), d suitable consecutive base cases can cover all residue-class chains. If a recurrence depends on the previous two terms, verify at least the two required initial values and ensure all referenced indices are in the established range.
proof_strong_induction__multibase_induct.explanation: The number of base cases depends on the actual recurrence structure; strong induction does not always require exactly two. Identifying the starting point reachable by each recurrence chain prevents omitted index classes.
notation: Decreasing by 3: three consecutive base cases are commonly used.
A second-order recurrence: usually check two initial values first.
proof_strong_induction__multibase_induct.example: To represent all n≥8 using denominations 3 and 5, first verify 8, 9, and 10. Then, whenever n−3 is in the established range, add one denomination-3 ticket.
common_mistakes: Using one base case with a fixed step size and claiming coverage of all integers.
Ignoring the requirement on n−2 at the smallest n in a second-order recurrence.

set_operation.title: Set operations
set_operation.summary: Set operations are defined by membership; complements require a fixed universal set.
set_operation.definition: For sets A and B within the same universal set U, A∪B contains elements in at least one of the two sets, A∩B contains elements in both, and A\B contains elements in A but not B. The complement of A is U\A. The symmetric difference is A△B=(A\B)∪(B\A). The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A.
set_operation.explanation: To prove two sets equal, show for arbitrary x that membership on the left is equivalent to membership on the right. Union and intersection satisfy commutative, associative, and distributive laws. De Morgan’s laws turn the complement of a union into an intersection of complements, and the complement of an intersection into a union of complements. Difference is generally not commutative. For finite sets, |A∪B|=|A|+|B|−|A∩B|; if |A|=n, then |P(A)|=2^n.
notation: A⊆B means every element of A belongs to B; A∈B means A itself is an element of B.
A^c=U\A; (A∪B)^c=A^c∩B^c.
∅ is the empty set; {∅} is a set containing one element.
common_mistakes: Discussing a complement without specifying the universal set.
Confusing A∈B with A⊆B, or treating ∅ and {∅} as the same set.
Failing to subtract the double-counted intersection when counting a union.

set_operation__complement.title: Complements and De Morgan’s laws
set_operation__complement.summary: Complements depend on a fixed universal set and interchange unions with intersections.
set_operation__complement.definition: Fix a universal set U with A⊆U. The complement of A is A^c=U\A. De Morgan’s laws state (A∪B)^c=A^c∩B^c and (A∩B)^c=A^c∪B^c.
set_operation__complement.explanation: Elements of a complement must lie in U; enlarging U changes the complement of the same A. De Morgan’s laws can be proved by translating nonmembership in a union or intersection into logical negation and comparing membership element by element.
notation: (A^c)^c=A; A∪A^c=U; A∩A^c=∅.
All sets in the same complement identity must use the same universal set.
set_operation__complement.example: If U={1,2,3} and A={1}, then A^c={2,3}. Changing the universal set to {1,2,3,4} also adds 4 to the complement.
common_mistakes: Finding a complement without fixing the universal set.
Negating an intersection but still intersecting the complements, without interchanging union and intersection.

set_operation__difference.title: Set difference
set_operation__difference.summary: A set difference retains elements of the first set that are not in the second.
set_operation__difference.definition: A\B={x｜x∈A and x∉B}. The second set need not be a subset of the first.
set_operation__difference.explanation: Difference is generally not commutative. A\B and B\A are disjoint, and A splits into the disjoint sets A\B and A∩B. With a fixed universal set, difference can also be written as the intersection of A with the complement of B, namely A∩B^c.
notation: A\B=A∩B^c, with complements relative to the same universal set.
common_mistakes: Reversing the set from which elements are removed and the set being removed.
Adding elements of B that were not originally in A to the result.

set_operation__inclusion_exclusion.title: Inclusion-exclusion for finite sets
set_operation__inclusion_exclusion.summary: Inclusion-exclusion corrects repeated counting by alternately adding and subtracting intersections.
set_operation__inclusion_exclusion.definition: Finite sets A, B, and C satisfy |A∪B∪C|=|A|+|B|+|C|−|A∩B|−|A∩C|−|B∩C|+|A∩B∩C|.
set_operation__inclusion_exclusion.explanation: Pairwise intersections include the triple intersection. Thus the three-set formula subtracts the three pairwise overlaps and adds the triple intersection back once. The number belonging to exactly two sets is the sum of the three pairwise intersection sizes minus three times the triple intersection size.
notation: Number in exactly two sets = |A∩B|+|A∩C|+|B∩C|−3|A∩B∩C|.
set_operation__inclusion_exclusion.example: If the three individual sizes are 10, 9, and 8, the pairwise intersection sizes are 4, 3, and 2, and the triple intersection size is 1, then the union contains 19 people and 6 people belong to exactly two sets.
common_mistakes: Interpreting pairwise intersection counts as counts of those in exactly two sets.
Forgetting to add the final triple-intersection term when counting a union.

set_operation__intersection.title: Intersection
set_operation__intersection.summary: An intersection requires elements to satisfy both membership conditions.
set_operation__intersection.definition: A∩B={x｜x∈A and x∈B}. If A∩B=∅, A and B are called disjoint.
set_operation__intersection.explanation: Intersection is commutative, associative, and idempotent, and union and intersection distribute over one another. With a fixed universal set U, A∩U=A. An empty intersection does not mean that both sets themselves are empty.
notation: A⊆B if and only if A∩B=A.
set_operation__intersection.example: {1,2}∩{2,3}={2}. Both {1} and {2} are nonempty, but their intersection is empty.
common_mistakes: Treating an intersection as a union.
Concluding that each set is empty from their intersection being empty.

set_operation__membership.title: Elements and membership
set_operation__membership.summary: Membership relates an object to a set containing that object as an element.
set_operation__membership.definition: x∈A means the object x is an element of A; x∉A means it is not. A set can itself be an element of another set.
set_operation__membership.explanation: A set is determined by its elements; changing their written order or repeating an element does not change the set. If an element is itself a set, its internal members do not automatically become elements of the outer set. The empty set has no elements, but another set may contain it as an element.
notation: x∈A and x⊆A express relations at different levels.
∅ and {∅} differ: their sizes are 0 and 1, respectively.
common_mistakes: Treating internal members of a set-valued element as elements of the outer set.
Believing that the empty set cannot be an element of another set.

set_operation__power_set.title: Power sets and counting subsets
set_operation__power_set.summary: A power set has all subsets of a set as its elements.
set_operation__power_set.definition: P(A)={X｜X⊆A} is called the power set of A. If A has n elements, each element may either be included in or excluded from a subset, so |P(A)|=2^n.
set_operation__power_set.explanation: The empty set and A itself always belong to P(A). A finite set has 2^n−1 nonempty subsets and 2^n−1 proper subsets; for n≥1, it has 2^n−2 nonempty proper subsets. P(A) and A are sets at different levels, so their element types must be distinguished.
notation: X∈P(A) is equivalent to X⊆A.
set_operation__power_set.example: If A={p,q}, then P(A)={∅,{p},{q},{p,q}}. Its nonempty proper subsets are exactly {p} and {q}.
common_mistakes: Writing the size of the power set as n².
Applying the formula 2^n−2, which requires n≥1, to the nonempty proper subsets of the empty set.

set_operation__subset.title: Subsets, proper subsets, and set equality
set_operation__subset.summary: The subset condition requires every element of one set to belong to another.
set_operation__subset.definition: A⊆B means every x∈A also satisfies x∈B. If additionally A≠B, A is a proper subset of B. A=B if and only if A⊆B and B⊆A.
set_operation__subset.explanation: The empty set is a subset of every set because no element can violate the condition. Proving inclusion requires considering an arbitrary element, rather than finding just one common element. Mutual inclusion splits set equality into two explicit implications.
notation: A⊊B means A⊆B and A≠B.
X∈P(A) is equivalent to X⊆A.
set_operation__subset.example: For A={∅,{1}}, {∅}⊆A but {∅}∈A is false. The set {1} is an element of A, whereas 1 is not.
common_mistakes: Interchanging ∈ and ⊆.
Proving inclusion in only one direction and asserting that the sets are equal.

set_operation__symmetric_difference.title: Symmetric difference
set_operation__symmetric_difference.summary: The symmetric difference retains elements belonging to exactly one of two sets.
set_operation__symmetric_difference.explanation: Symmetric difference is commutative and associative, and A△A=∅. For two finite sets, |A△B|=|A|+|B|−2|A∩B|; common elements must be removed completely.
notation: x∈A△B if and only if exactly one of the two membership conditions for x holds.
common_mistakes: Treating symmetric difference as union.
Subtracting the intersection only once when counting.

set_operation__union.title: Union
set_operation__union.summary: A union retains elements belonging to at least one of two sets.
set_operation__union.definition: A∪B={x｜x∈A or x∈B}, where “or” allows membership in both sets.
set_operation__union.explanation: Union is commutative, associative, and idempotent. Common elements must not be counted twice in a finite union; for two sets, |A∪B|=|A|+|B|−|A∩B|.
notation: A∪∅=A; A∪A=A.
A⊆B if and only if A∪B=B.
common_mistakes: Interpreting “or” exclusively, as “exactly one.”
Counting elements belonging to both sets twice.

relation_cartesian.title: Cartesian products and relations
relation_cartesian.summary: A binary relation is a subset of a Cartesian product; both the left and right object sets must be specified.
relation_cartesian.definition: The Cartesian product of A and B is A×B={(a,b)｜a∈A, b∈B}; its elements are ordered pairs. A binary relation R from A to B is any subset of A×B. If A=B, R is called a binary relation on A.
relation_cartesian.explanation: A relation may be represented by a set of ordered pairs, a 0–1 matrix, or a directed graph. The element orders corresponding to matrix rows and columns must be specified first; graph vertices and arrow directions represent ordered pairs. A relation need not use every left endpoint, and one left endpoint may be related to several right endpoints. Those additional restrictions concern functions. For finite sets, |A×B|=|A||B|, and there are 2^(|A||B|) relations from A to B.
notation: (a,b)=(c,d) if and only if a=c and b=d.
R⊆A×B; the empty relation ∅ is also valid.
If either A or B is empty, then A×B=∅.
relation_cartesian.example: If A={1,2} and B={x,y}, then A×B has four ordered pairs. R={(1,x),(1,y)} is a relation from A to B even though 1 is related to two elements and 2 to none.
common_mistakes: Treating the ordered pair (a,b) as the unordered set {a,b}.
Requiring a general relation to be a function.
Omitting the sets and element orders represented by the rows and columns of a relation matrix.

relation_cartesian__binary_relation.title: Binary relations and their types
relation_cartesian__binary_relation.summary: A binary relation is any subset of a specified Cartesian product.
relation_cartesian__binary_relation.definition: A binary relation from A to B is a set R⊆A×B; a relation on A is a subset of A×A. Both the empty set and the whole Cartesian product are valid relations.
relation_cartesian__binary_relation.explanation: A relation need not associate each element of A with an element of B, nor need an associated element be unique. Pairs with the wrong component types cannot form a relation from the specified A to B, even if they are correctly written as ordered pairs.
notation: aRb abbreviates (a,b)∈R.
All relations from A to B form P(A×B).
relation_cartesian__binary_relation.example: For A={1,2} and B={a}, ∅, {(1,a)}, and {(1,a),(2,a)} are all valid relations.
common_mistakes: Imposing the totality and single-valuedness requirements of functions on general relations.
Adding pairs from B×A to a relation specified as a subset of A×B.

relation_cartesian__cartesian_product.title: Cartesian product
relation_cartesian__cartesian_product.summary: A Cartesian product lists all ordered pairs drawn from two specified sets.
relation_cartesian__cartesian_product.definition: A×B={(a,b)｜a∈A and b∈B}. For finite sets, |A×B|=|A||B|.
relation_cartesian__cartesian_product.explanation: The first component comes from A and the second from B, so the factor order determines the component types. If either factor is empty, the product is empty. Although A×B and B×A have equal numbers of elements, they need not be equal as sets.
common_mistakes: Omitting a combination of components.
Replacing set equality with equality of product cardinalities.

relation_cartesian__ordered_pair.title: Ordered pairs and their equality
relation_cartesian__ordered_pair.summary: An ordered pair distinguishes its components by position; their order cannot be interchanged arbitrarily.
relation_cartesian__ordered_pair.definition: (a,b)=(c,d) if and only if a=c and b=d. The first and second components may be equal and may themselves be sets.
relation_cartesian__ordered_pair.explanation: The unordered set {a,b} records no order and removes repetitions; the ordered pair (a,b) always retains two positions. Relations use ordered pairs as their basic records, rather than unordered two-element sets.
notation: (a,b)=(b,a) if and only if a=b.
(a,a) is still a valid ordered pair.
common_mistakes: Interpreting an ordered pair as a two-element set.
Believing a pair is invalid when its two components are equal.

relation_cartesian__relation_counting.title: Counting binary relations and constrained relations
relation_cartesian__relation_counting.summary: For every ordered pair in the Cartesian product, independently choose whether to include it.
relation_cartesian__relation_counting.definition: If finite sets have |A|=m and |B|=n, then A×B has mn candidate ordered pairs. Each subset defines a relation, so there are 2^(mn) relations in total.
relation_cartesian__relation_counting.explanation: If some pairs must be included and others must be excluded, with no conflicting requirements, only the remaining pairs are free choices. If every element of A must relate to at least one element of B, choose a nonempty subset in each row; the general counting formula for unrestricted relations does not apply directly.
notation: There is exactly one empty relation; when mn=0, it is still the unique relation.
Fixing the statuses of k distinct candidate pairs without conflict leaves 2^(mn−k) choices.
relation_cartesian__relation_counting.example: If |A|=2 and |B|=2, there are 16 relations. Requiring one pair to be present and a different pair to be absent leaves only 2²=4 relations.
common_mistakes: Confusing the number of relations with mn, the number of candidate ordered pairs.
Using the exponential formula despite simultaneously requiring the same pair to be both present and absent.

relation_cartesian__representations.title: Boolean matrix representation of a relation
relation_cartesian__representations.summary: A relation matrix records whether each association exists, using a fixed row and column order.
relation_cartesian__representations.definition: For A=(a₁,…,a_m) and B=(b₁,…,b_n), the matrix M_R of R⊆A×B is the m×n 0–1 matrix with M_R[i,j]=1 if and only if (a_i,b_j)∈R.
relation_cartesian__representations.explanation: The row and column orders are part of the representation: reordering changes the matrix without changing the abstract relation. Taking the inverse relation corresponds to transposition. Composition uses Boolean matrix multiplication, with AND for multiplication and OR for combining terms; multiple realizations of the same relation pair are recorded as just 1.
notation: R⁻¹ corresponds to the n×m matrix M_R^T.
0 means the ordered pair is not selected by the relation.
relation_cartesian__representations.example: For A=(u,v) and B=(0,1), a matrix with rows (1,0) and (1,1) represents R={(u,0),(v,0),(v,1)}.
common_mistakes: Omitting the object orders corresponding to the rows and columns.
Using the number of different intermediate paths between the same endpoints as a Boolean matrix entry.

relation_operation.title: Operations on relations
relation_operation.summary: Relations admit inversion, composition, and powers; composition order must follow an explicit definition.
relation_operation.definition: For R⊆A×B and S⊆B×C, the convention here is S∘R={(a,c)｜there exists b∈B with (a,b)∈R and (b,c)∈S}: first follow R, then S. The inverse relation is R⁻¹={(b,a)｜(a,b)∈R}. Relations in the same Cartesian product also admit union, intersection, difference, and complement relative to that product.
relation_operation.explanation: For a relation R on A, define R⁰=I_A and R^(k+1)=R∘R^k, where I_A={(a,a)｜a∈A}. Membership (x,y)∈R^k means there exists a relation chain of length exactly k; elements may be revisited. It does not count such chains. Composition is associative and usually not commutative; relation matrices use Boolean multiplication for composition rather than ordinary counting multiplication.
notation: S∘R: first R, then S. If a textbook uses a different symbol convention, follow the definition given in the problem.
(S∘R)⁻¹=R⁻¹∘S⁻¹.
I_A is the identity relation on A.
relation_operation.example: On A={1,2,3}, let R={(1,2),(2,3)}. Then R²={(1,3)}, since the only two-step chain is 1→2→3. R³=∅ because no edge continues from 3.
common_mistakes: Computing S∘R in written left-to-right order.
Reversing arrows for an inverse relation without exchanging the left and right object sets.
Treating the number of ordered pairs in R^k as the total number of relation chains of length k.

relation_operation__complement_relation.title: Complement of a relation
relation_operation__complement_relation.summary: A relation complement is taken relative to the specified full Cartesian product.
relation_operation__complement_relation.definition: For R⊆A×B, its complement relation is (A×B)\R. If R is a relation on A, the universal set is A×A.
relation_operation__complement_relation.explanation: The inverse relation swaps components, whereas the complement changes whether each candidate ordered pair is selected. Complementing the matrix swaps every 0 and 1 while preserving its dimensions and the object orders of rows and columns.
notation: R and its complement are disjoint and their union is A×B.
The complement has size |A||B|−|R| in the finite case.
relation_operation__complement_relation.example: For A={1,2} and R={(1,2)}, the complement relation on A is {(1,1),(2,1),(2,2)}.
common_mistakes: Confusing the complement relation with the inverse relation.
Overlooking diagonal pairs or other candidate pairs in A×B.

q01.title: Identifying propositions
q01.statement: Which of the following statements is a false proposition?
q01.explanation: “9 is even” is a statement with a definite truth value, and it is false. A is an imperative sentence; D contains an unspecified free variable x and is not yet a definite proposition; B is a true proposition.
q01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing C. Explaining that A is not a declarative proposition and that D contains a free variable may be used as feedback on the reasoning.

options.text: Please write this problem on paper.

q02.title: Truth value of an implication
q02.statement: When proposition p is false and proposition q is true, what is the truth value of p→q?
q02.explanation: An implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. When p is false, p→q is true whether q is true or false.

options.text: p and q must both be true

q03.title: An equivalent form of implication
q03.statement: By the equivalence law for implication, p→q is equivalent to ______.
q03.explanation: p→q is false only when p is true and q is false. ¬p∨q is also false in exactly that case, so the two have the same truth value under every truth assignment.
q03.grading_criteria: Full credit for “¬p∨q” or a correctly written expression with the same meaning.

q04.title: Negating a universal statement
q04.statement: Negate the proposition “For every integer n, n²≥0.” Retain the complete domain.
q04.answer_text: There exists an integer n such that n²<0.
q04.explanation: Negating a universal quantifier changes it to an existential quantifier and negates the predicate: ¬(∀n∈ℤ, n²≥0) is equivalent to ∃n∈ℤ such that n²<0.
q04.grading_criteria: Both “there exists an integer n” and “n²<0” are required. An inequality without the existential quantifier does not receive full credit.

q05.title: Set operations
q05.statement: Let U={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} be the universal set, A={1,2,3,5}, and B={2,4,5,7}. Find A∪B, A∩B, A∖B, and the complement of A in U.
q05.explanation: The union contains elements belonging to at least one set; the intersection contains only elements belonging to both sets; A∖B contains elements of A that are not in B. The complement must be calculated relative to the specified universal set U.
q05.grading_criteria: Each of the four results is worth 25%. Different orders of the same set of elements are accepted.

q06.title: Properties of a relation
q06.statement: Let A={1,2,3} and R={(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)}. Which of the following properties hold?
q06.explanation: All three diagonal pairs are in R, so R is reflexive. The non-diagonal pair (1,2) has its reverse (2,1), so R is symmetric. Since 1≠2 and the relation holds in both directions, R is not antisymmetric. Checking compositions of pairs within {1,2}, together with the diagonal pair for 3, shows that R is transitive.
q06.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting A, B, and D and excluding C. Extra selections or omissions receive partial credit.

q07.title: Equivalence classes of congruence
q07.statement: On the integers define a relation by: a is related to b if and only if 4 divides a−b. List all its distinct equivalence classes, and determine whether 7 and −1 belong to the same class.
q07.answer_text: There are four equivalence classes, [0], [1], [2], and [3], consisting respectively of integers with remainders 0, 1, 2, and 3 modulo 4. Since 7−(−1)=8 is divisible by 4, 7 and −1 belong to the same class.
q07.explanation: Two integers are congruent modulo 4 if and only if they have the same remainder upon division by 4. The only possible remainders are 0, 1, 2, and 3, so there are exactly four equivalence classes.
q07.grading_criteria: Describing the four classes by their remainders is worth 70%; correctly placing 7 and −1 in the same class and giving their difference is worth 30%.

q08.title: Injectivity and surjectivity
q08.statement: Let f:ℤ→ℤ be defined by f(n)=2n+1. Prove that f is injective but not surjective.
q08.answer_text: Injectivity: If f(a)=f(b), then 2a+1=2b+1, hence a=b, so f is injective. Failure of surjectivity: Take any even integer 2k. If an integer n satisfied f(n)=2k, then 2n+1=2k would give n=k−1/2, which is not an integer. Thus no even integer is in the image, and f is not surjective.
q08.explanation: For injectivity, equal function values must imply equal inputs. To disprove surjectivity it suffices to find one element of the codomain with no preimage. Here every even integer has no integer preimage.
q08.grading_criteria: A correct proof of injectivity is worth 40%; identifying even integers as having no preimages and explaining why is worth 60%. A single input-output example cannot replace a proof.

q09.title: A partial order given by divisibility
q09.statement: On A={1,2,3,6}, define the relation “a divides b.” Give the least and greatest elements of this partially ordered set, and identify a pair of incomparable elements.
q09.answer_text: The least element is 1 and the greatest element is 6; 2 and 3 are incomparable.
q09.explanation: 1 divides every element of A, so 1 is the least element. Every element of A divides 6, so 6 is the greatest element. Neither 2 divides 3 nor 3 divides 2, so they are incomparable.
q09.grading_criteria: Full credit requires all three conclusions to be correct. Distinguish a least element from a minimal element.

q10.title: The handshaking theorem
q10.statement: A finite undirected graph has four vertices of degrees 3, 2, 2, and 1, respectively. Find its number of edges.
q10.explanation: By the handshaking theorem, the sum of all vertex degrees is twice the number of edges. The degree sum is 3+2+2+1=8, so the number of edges is 8÷2=4.
q10.grading_criteria: Full credit for stating the handshaking theorem and calculating 4 edges.

q11.title: Connected components
q11.statement: An undirected graph has vertex set {A,B,C,D} and edge set {{A,B},{B,C}}. List all its connected components.
q11.answer_text: There are two connected components: one consists of vertices A, B, and C and edges {A,B} and {B,C}; the other is the isolated vertex D.
q11.explanation: There are paths connecting A, B, and C, so they belong to one connected component. D has no connection to any other vertex and forms a component on its own.
q11.grading_criteria: Full credit for identifying the two components {A,B,C} and {D}. Do not omit the isolated vertex.

q12.title: Edges of a tree and deleting an edge
q12.statement: A tree has 9 vertices. How many edges does it have? How many connected components result after any one of its edges is deleted?
q12.answer_text: The original tree has 8 edges. Deleting any edge splits the graph into two connected components.
q12.explanation: A tree with n vertices has n−1 edges, so this tree has 9−1=8 edges. Every edge of a tree is a bridge; deleting it disconnects the graph into exactly two connected components.
q12.grading_criteria: The number of edges and the number of connected components are each worth 50%. Explain that every edge of a tree is a bridge.

q13.title: Applying the pigeonhole principle
q13.statement: Prove that among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month.
q13.answer_text: View the 12 months as 12 boxes and the 13 people as 13 objects. Put each person into the box corresponding to their birth month. Since there are 13 objects and only 12 boxes, the pigeonhole principle implies that some box contains at least 2 people. Therefore at least two people were born in the same month.
q13.explanation: Identify the objects and boxes: the people are the objects and the months are the boxes. There is no need to identify the particular two people or to know how many people were born in each month.
q13.grading_criteria: Correctly matching 13 people to 12 months is worth 40%; correctly applying the pigeonhole principle and concluding the proof is worth 60%.

q14.title: Proving the sum of odd integers by induction
q14.statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that for every positive integer n, 1+3+5+⋯+(2n−1)=n².
q14.answer_text: Base case: For n=1, the left side is 1 and the right side is 1²=1, so the claim holds. Induction hypothesis: Assume the claim holds for n=k, that is, 1+3+⋯+(2k−1)=k². Inductive step: For n=k+1, the left side is k²+[2(k+1)−1]=k²+2k+1=(k+1)², which equals the right side. Thus the claim holds for k+1. By mathematical induction, it holds for every positive integer n.
q14.explanation: The proof must include a base case, an induction hypothesis, and an inductive step. In the inductive step, add the (k+1)st odd integer, 2k+1, to the sum of the first k terms.
q14.grading_criteria: Base case: 20%; correct induction hypothesis: 20%; correct algebra in the inductive step: 40%; complete conclusion: 20%.

q_logic_truth_01.title: Open sentences and closed propositions
q_logic_truth_01.statement: Let n be an integer variable that has not been assigned a value. Which of the following is itself a closed proposition?
q_logic_truth_01.explanation: “31 is odd” asserts a property of a fixed integer and has a definite truth value. In A, n remains free; C is a command; D is a question.
q_logic_truth_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only B. The explanation should distinguish free variables, imperative sentences, and questions.

q_logic_truth_02.title: Does an unknown truth value prevent a statement from being a proposition?
q_logic_truth_02.statement: A student has not tested whether the fixed integer N=10^20+39 is prime. Is the statement “N is prime” a proposition? Discuss only whether it is a proposition; no primality test is required.
q_logic_truth_02.answer_text: Yes. N is fixed, so the statement has a definite truth value, true or false. The student’s present lack of knowledge does not prevent it from being a proposition.
q_logic_truth_02.explanation: The criterion is whether a statement has a definite truth value, not whether someone already knows that value. There is no need to claim that N is actually prime or composite.
q_logic_truth_02.grading_criteria: Answering “yes” is worth 40%; explaining that N is fixed and that an unknown truth value is still a truth value is worth 60%.

q_logic_truth_03.title: Closing an open sentence by assignment and quantification
q_logic_truth_03.statement: Over the integers, let P(n) mean n²=n. Give the truth values of P(0), P(2), and “For every integer n, P(n),” and explain how these differ from P(n) with n unassigned.
q_logic_truth_03.answer_text: P(0) is true because 0²=0. P(2) is false because 4≠2. The universal statement is false, with n=2 as a counterexample. P(n) with n unassigned is an open sentence; it cannot be assigned a single truth value without an assignment or a quantifier.
q_logic_truth_03.explanation: The first two statements replace the free variable with a constant; the third binds it with a universal quantifier. All three are therefore closed propositions, but their truth values need not agree.
q_logic_truth_03.grading_criteria: Each of the three truth values is worth 20%; the universal counterexample and explanation of the open sentence together are worth 40%.

q_logic_truth_04.title: Truth values in a fixed context
q_logic_truth_04.statement: The context is the first lesson of Class A on October 12, 2026, and the attendance record shows 24 students present. Is “25 students in this class attended today’s first lesson” a proposition, and what is its truth value? If exactly 25 students attend on another day, making the same sentence true in that new context, is there a logical contradiction?
q_logic_truth_04.answer_text: In the given context, it is a proposition and is false. The statement on the other day concerns a different date and expresses a different specific fact. Different truth values in different contexts do not make one and the same proposition both true and false.
q_logic_truth_04.explanation: References such as “this class” and “today” depend on context. The class, date, and lesson must be fixed to interpret the assertion; these conditions must remain the same when comparing truth values.
q_logic_truth_04.grading_criteria: Identifying it as a false proposition is worth 40%; explaining that the two dates give different specific propositions and hence no contradiction is worth 60%.

q_logic_connectives_01.title: Evaluating compound connectives using parentheses
q_logic_connectives_01.statement: Suppose p is true and q is false. Evaluate (¬p∨q)∧(p∨¬q), giving the truth values at both levels of subformulas.
q_logic_connectives_01.answer_text: ¬p is false and ¬q is true. Thus ¬p∨q is false and p∨¬q is true, so the whole conjunction is false.
q_logic_connectives_01.explanation: Evaluate the negations first, then the two parenthesized formulas, and finally the conjunction. An outer ∧ is false whenever either component is false.
q_logic_connectives_01.grading_criteria: The two negations together are worth 20%; the two parenthesized formulas together are worth 40%; the final value false is worth 40%.

q_logic_connectives_02.title: Expressing that exactly one proposition holds
q_logic_connectives_02.statement: Let p and q be arbitrary propositions. Which formulas are true exactly when one of p and q is true? Select all correct options.
q_logic_connectives_02.explanation: A requires at least one to be true and excludes both being true. B lists the cases “p true, q false” and “p false, q true.” C is also true when both are true. D is true when both are true or both are false, so it has a different meaning.
q_logic_connectives_02.grading_criteria: Full credit for selecting both A and B and excluding C and D. Explaining the differences between exclusive disjunction, inclusive disjunction, and the biconditional can earn reasoning credit.

q_logic_connectives_03.title: Recovering an unknown truth value from a biconditional
q_logic_connectives_03.statement: The formula s↔(p∧q) is true, p is true, and s is false. Find the truth value of q and justify your answer.
q_logic_connectives_03.answer_text: q is false. A true biconditional requires s and p∧q to have the same truth value, so p∧q is false. Since p is true, the conjunction can be false only if q is false.
q_logic_connectives_03.explanation: A true biconditional does not mean that both sides are true; it also holds when both sides are false.
q_logic_connectives_03.grading_criteria: Using equality of truth values to show the conjunction is false is worth 50%; using p true to conclude q false is worth 50%.

q_logic_connectives_04.title: The direction of an “only if” condition and its converse
q_logic_connectives_04.statement: Let s, l, and n mean “submission succeeds,” “the user is logged in,” and “the network is available,” respectively. Express “Submission can succeed only if the user is logged in and the network is available” as a formula. Does it imply “If the user is logged in and the network is available, submission succeeds”? If not, give a counterexample assignment.
q_logic_connectives_04.answer_text: The original statement is s→(l∧n). It does not imply (l∧n)→s. Set s=false, l=true, n=true; the original formula is true and the converse is false.
q_logic_connectives_04.explanation: An “only if” statement gives necessary conditions for success, without giving sufficient conditions. Other restrictions may apply in addition to login and network availability.
q_logic_connectives_04.grading_criteria: Symbolization: 40%; identifying that the converse does not follow: 20%; a counterexample making the original true and converse false: 40%.

q_logic_truth_table_01.title: Distinct letters determine the number of truth-table rows
q_logic_truth_table_01.statement: A formula contains exactly five distinct propositional letters p, q, r, s, and t, with p occurring three times. Its complete truth table has ______ rows.
q_logic_truth_table_01.explanation: Each of the five distinct letters has two possible truth values, giving 2^5=32 assignments. Every occurrence of p must have the same value within an assignment, so repetitions do not add independent variables.
q_logic_truth_table_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for 32. Explaining that only distinct propositional letters are counted can earn reasoning credit.

q_logic_truth_table_02.title: The complete truth column for a three-variable implication chain
q_logic_truth_table_02.statement: Let F=(p→q)∧(q→r). Give its eight truth values in the order (p,q,r)=000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111, and list the assignments making F true. Here 0 means false and 1 means true.
q_logic_truth_table_02.answer_text: The truth column is 1,1,0,1,0,0,0,1. The true assignments are 000, 001, 011, and 111, for a total of 4.
q_logic_truth_table_02.explanation: For both implications to be true, p=1,q=0 and q=1,r=0 must both be excluded. Hence the values must satisfy p≤q≤r, giving exactly the four listed rows.
q_logic_truth_table_02.grading_criteria: The complete eight-row column is worth 80%; listing exactly the four true assignments without omissions is worth 20%.

q_logic_truth_table_03.title: Classifying a disjunction of opposite implications
q_logic_truth_table_03.statement: For arbitrary propositions p and q, how is (p→q)∨(q→p) classified?
q_logic_truth_table_03.explanation: In the order 00, 01, 10, 11, its truth values are 1, 1, 1, 1. In the only case where p→q is false, namely p=1,q=0, q→p is true. Thus the whole disjunction cannot be false.
q_logic_truth_table_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for choosing only A. A truth table or an explanation using the incompatible conditions for falsity is accepted.
